FOR GROWN-UPS

What does “looking closely” mean?

The problem. Some children find it difficult to distinguish similar pictures, check more than one feature, or find a target among alternatives. For example, a child may select a blue fish instead of a blue leaf because color captures their attention. A busy display, unfamiliar instructions, or difficult controls can also cause mistakes.

Our goal: visual discrimination. The child learns to look at a model, compare choices, notice the relevant similarities and differences, and check before choosing. We practice shape, color, size, direction, pattern, parts, position, and arrangements. These are visual comparisons, not lessons in letter sounds, language, or counting.

How the 25 games build up

Games 1–4 introduce basic matching and single features. Games 5–8 focus on direction and internal details. Games 9–10 combine features. Games 11–15 introduce silhouettes, outlines, reflections, dot positions, and spacing. Games 16–20 extend search, partial-picture matching, shape constancy, fine details, and three-object arrangements. Games 21–25 add active sorting, face-up pairing, building a mushroom to match, turning a leaf, and finding a changed picture. All examples remain visible; there is no hidden-card memory test. Each game has a model and five rounds. The order is a suggestion, not a developmental assessment.

Who might benefit?

Some autistic children may need help attending to all relevant features rather than one striking detail. Children with developmental delay or intellectual disability, including some children with Down syndrome, may need repeated, carefully scaffolded matching practice. Children with language or speech difficulties and children who use AAC can respond without speaking. These are reasons to consider the task, not evidence that the course treats those conditions. Many children in these groups will not need it.

Choose by observed need. Start with a comfortable game. If matching is already easy, move on; do not require completion. Watch for fatigue or distress. Slow or incorrect responses may reflect motor access, vision, unclear instructions, or overload rather than poor discrimination.

Make it accessible

Use a demonstration and allow a pointing response with adult assistance if tapping is difficult. Buttons also work with keyboard Tab and Enter/Space. Try short sessions with breaks. No dragging or timed responses are required. Color-only games may be inaccessible with color-vision differences; skip them. Children with low vision or cerebral visual impairment may need individualized advice from their vision team; shadows, partial pictures, and larger arrays can be especially difficult. This course is not vision therapy.

AAC access comes first. Matching games must never be used as a prerequisite for communication support. Keep the child’s usual AAC system available and use their established access method. This app does not provide individualized AAC assessment or eye-gaze access.

What counts as progress?

Look for accurate choices with less help, across new examples and on a later day. Try a real-world comparison, such as finding a matching toy, to see whether the skill carries over. The model stays visible so hidden-picture memory is not the target. In the five hands-on games, an independent round means completing all its steps without a retry or hint. Selecting parts or turning an object is exploration; only an incorrect submitted answer or incorrect pair/home counts as a retry. Hints and first-try answers are recorded separately; completing five rounds means practice finished, not mastery.

Relationship to reading. Visual discrimination is useful in many learning activities, but these games have not been evaluated as reading interventions. Transfer to reading is unproven. They do not diagnose or treat dyslexia, and a child does not need to finish them before receiving reading instruction.

Research and professional guidance

Research supports carefully designed matching and discrimination teaching for specific tasks. It does not validate this particular course or establish benefits for every diagnostic group.
